blocks.prompt: The Person Who Flies the Plane
blocks.text: A pilot is the person who flies a plane. Before the plane leaves, the pilot walks all the way around it. She checks the wings, the wheels, and the lights. Then she climbs into the front. This part of the plane is called the cockpit. It has more buttons than you can count. The pilot pushes the engines to full power, and the plane rolls faster and faster down the runway. The wings lift it up. High in the sky, the pilot talks to people on the ground by radio. They help keep every plane far apart and safe.

blocks.prompt: What a Pilot Really Does
blocks.text: A pilot is trained to fly an airplane, but flying is only part of the job. Long before takeoff, the pilot studies the weather along the whole route. Storms, wind, and ice can all change the plan. Next comes the walkaround, when the pilot inspects the plane from the outside, checking the wings, engines, and tires for anything wrong. Inside the cockpit, the pilot and the co-pilot run through a checklist together. They read each item out loud so nothing is forgotten. On most flights there are two pilots for a reason: if one needs a break, the other can fly. To take off, the pilot pushes the engines to full power and pulls back gently once the plane is fast enough. Air rushing over the curved wings creates lift, and the plane climbs. High up, a computer called the autopilot can hold the plane steady, but the pilot still watches everything and lands the plane by hand. Landing softly on a narrow runway is the hardest skill a pilot learns.

blocks.prompt: Flying the Machine
blocks.text: Most people think a pilot spends the whole flight steering the plane by hand. The truth is more interesting. Flying a modern airliner is mostly about managing systems, making decisions, and staying ready for the moment when a machine cannot decide for itself. The work begins on the ground. Pilots study the route, the weather, and how much fuel the plane will need. They calculate the plane's weight, because a heavier plane needs a longer runway and more speed to lift off. Then comes the walkaround, an outside inspection of the wings, engines, and tires. Takeoff and landing are flown by hand, and they demand the most skill. In between, the autopilot usually holds the course while the pilots monitor the instruments, talk with air traffic control, and plan ahead. Air traffic controllers on the ground act like traffic officers of the sky, keeping every plane a safe distance from the others. The reason planes fly at all comes down to their wings. As the plane speeds forward, air moving over the curved top of the wing lowers the pressure there, and the higher pressure below pushes the wing up. That upward force is called lift. When lift is greater than the plane's weight, the plane rises. A pilot's calm matters as much as skill. When something goes wrong, passengers look to a steady voice on the radio, and training takes over.

blocks.prompt: The Person in the Captain's Hat
blocks.text: Look into the cockpit of an airliner and you will usually see two people, not one. The one in the left seat, wearing four stripes on each sleeve, is the captain, who carries final responsibility for the flight. In the right seat sits the first officer, sometimes called the co-pilot, who flies the plane just as often. The two trade duties, and on a long journey they take turns resting, because a tired pilot is a dangerous one. Becoming a pilot takes years. A person must earn a license, pass medical exams, and log hundreds of hours in the air before an airline will hire them. Even then the learning never stops. Pilots return to training rooms every few months to practice emergencies in a simulator, a machine that copies the cockpit so exactly that a pilot can rehearse an engine failure that they hope never to face in real life. Most of a flight is calm. After a hand-flown takeoff, the crew engages the autopilot and settles into a rhythm of watching instruments, tracking fuel, and speaking with a chain of air traffic controllers who hand the plane from one region to the next. The controllers keep aircraft spaced safely apart, like a careful conversation where only one voice speaks at a time. The quiet is the point. Aviation is built to be boring on purpose. Every checklist, every backup system, and every rule was written to remove surprises, and many were written after accidents taught hard lessons. A pilot's real job is to notice the small thing early, the odd reading or the wrong sound, and to act before it becomes a large thing. Then comes the landing. Autopilots can land in some conditions, but pilots practice landing by hand for a reason. Bringing a heavy machine down through gusting wind and setting its wheels gently onto a strip of concrete, at the right speed and the right angle, is a skill that rewards thousands of hours of practice. When it is done well, the passengers barely notice, and that is exactly how a pilot wants it.

meta.templateLabel: The Person in the Captain's Hat

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Two pilots so no single failure brings the plane down
Simulators let crews rehearse disasters safely
Lift depends on speed; too slow and the wing stalls
Systems are doubled and tripled as backups
The industry studies its failures in public

blocks.prompt: Forever Calm: How Pilots Are Built for the Worst Moment
blocks.text: The strangest thing about a modern airline pilot is how little of the job looks like flying. For most of a journey the aircraft flies itself, holding altitude and heading under the guidance of an autopilot, while two trained people sit and watch. To an outsider this can look like idleness. It is the opposite. The entire profession is designed around a single idea: that the rare, dangerous moment is the one that matters, and that everything before it exists to make that moment survivable. Start with who is in the cockpit. The captain, marked by four stripes, holds final authority, but the first officer beside them flies the plane on roughly half of all legs. This is deliberate. Two qualified pilots mean that no single failure, of a person or a machine, is likely to bring the aircraft down. On long routes they rest in turns, because fatigue quietly erodes judgment in ways a pilot cannot always feel. Becoming one of these people is slow work. A pilot earns a license, passes repeated medical checks, and logs hundreds of flight hours, and even that is only the beginning. Every few months, airline pilots return to a simulator, a full-motion copy of the cockpit precise enough to rehearse disasters. There they practice engine failures, fires, and sudden loss of pressure, over and over, so that if the real thing ever comes, their hands already know the answer. The goal is to turn panic into routine. Understanding how the plane stays up helps explain the caution. A wing works because air flowing over its curved upper surface moves faster and presses down less than the slower air beneath, so the plane is pushed upward by a force called lift. Lift depends on speed. Fly too slowly and the smooth flow breaks apart, the wing stalls, and the lift vanishes. Much of a pilot's training is really the management of that narrow margin between fast enough and too slow. The culture of aviation reflects all of this. Checklists are read aloud so that no step lives only in a forgetful memory. Systems are doubled and tripled so that a broken part has a backup. Many of these rules exist because earlier accidents revealed a gap, and the industry has a habit, rare among human institutions, of studying its failures in public and rewriting the rules so the same failure cannot happen twice. That habit is the quiet heart of the passage worth noticing. Read again and you will see that almost every fact points the same direction: two pilots, endless practice, redundant systems, aloud checklists. The author is not merely describing a job. The author is building a case that safety in the air is not luck or the nerve of one heroic person, but a system engineered to catch mistakes before they grow. The pilot in the captain's hat is the visible tip of that system, and the reason a passenger can fall asleep at thirty-five thousand feet and never once wonder whether the wings will hold.
